parts.text:
You read part of an interview. An analyst asked one future user of a software service a series of questions. You decide, for each question, whether it follows up the answer given just before it.

A question follows up the previous answer when it asks about something that answer said: it asks the speaker to explain, give an example of, say more about, or say why of something the answer mentioned, or it picks up a particular thing the answer named. Wording does not matter; a question can follow up an answer without repeating any of its words.

A question does not follow up the previous answer when it turns to something that answer did not mention, even if the speaker said it in an earlier answer, even if it stays with the same broad subject, and even if it is a good question. A general question that could follow any answer, such as whether there is anything else, does not follow up either.

You receive the pairs of the interview after its first question: for each later question, the answer given just before it, and the question.

Reply with JSON only: an object with one key, "questions", a list with exactly one entry for every pair, in the same order. Each entry has "id", the question's id, and "follow_up", true or false.

Q2
The answer just before it: I don't know.
The question: What is the very first thing you did when you started your shift today?

Q3
The answer just before it: I don't know.
The question: Which of the drone companies do you work for, and what kind of drones do you look after?

Q4
The answer just before it: I don't know which specific drone operating company I work for, but we run a few hundred drones of several models from different manufacturers. These models differ in their carrying capacity, flight range on a full battery, the sensors they carry, and the charging connectors they use. My job involves keeping these drones and our charging equipment in working order.
The question: How do you find out which drones or charging equipment need your attention?

Q5
The answer just before it: I don't know.
The question: Who hands work to you, and who do you hand work to?

Q6
The answer just before it: I don't know.
The question: What tasks are involved in keeping the drones and charging equipment in working order?

Q7
The answer just before it: My work involves adding new drones to the fleet, retiring old ones, and setting up charging pads at our sites. I also take drones out of service for repairs, put them back when they are fixed, and send them to charge. Regulators can ask our company to show how our drones have been looked after.
The question: When regulators ask your company to show how the drones have been looked after, what exact details do you have to show them?

Q8
The answer just before it: I don't know.
The question: Thinking back over the last few months, what was your worst day on the job, and what made it so bad?

Q9
The answer just before it: I don't know about a specific worst day. However, it worries me that radio coverage is patchy around ports, industrial sites, and in bad weather, and that reports from drones can arrive late, out of order, more than once, or not at all.
The question: Can you give me a concrete example of a problem caused when drone reports arrive late, out of order, or not at all?

The answer just before it: I don't know.
The question: What do you check by hand today because you don't trust the automatic reports or current tools?

Q11
The answer just before it: I don't know.
The question: Right after something goes wrong with a drone or a charging pad, what do you need to know?

Q12
The answer just before it: I don't know.
The question: What are you afraid a new software service would get wrong in your work?

Q13
The answer just before it: I don't know what a new software service would get wrong in my work.
The question: When you set up charging pads at your sites or send drones to charge, what do you have to keep track of?

Q14
The answer just before it: I set up charging pads at our sites, and several connector types are in use that are not interchangeable. Each of our sites has a few dozen charging pads, and we never lend pads to another company.
The question: When you take a drone out of service for repairs or put it back in service, what happens to its schedule or how do dispatchers know?

Q15

The question: What information do you record when adding a new drone to the fleet or retiring an old one?

Q16
The answer just before it: I don't know.
The question: What kinds of reports do the drones send in, and what is in them?

Q17
The answer just before it: I don't know.
The question: How do you decide when a drone needs to be sent to charge or taken out of service?

Q18
The answer just before it: I don't know.
The question: What else do you know about your company's sites, charging pads, or fleet rules?

Q19
The answer just before it: Each company runs its own charging pads at its own sites, numbering a few dozen, and these pads are never lent to another company. Furthermore, several connector types are in use across our fleet, and they are not interchangeable.
The question: Is there anything else about your responsibilities, the equipment, or the rules you follow that we haven't covered yet?
